rv.q: This autobiographical musical about a young black man's search for artistic authenticity is a rock concert, a coming-of-age story and a meditation on identity rolled into one electrifying package.
Passing Strange is a theatrical memoir that works because it tells a specific story with universal resonance, and because Stew has the rare ability to make his personal journey feel like our own.

What's important is that the thing - part indie-rock concert, part boho-art project, part coming-of-age black-identity crisis, part hipster travelogue - is all smart and all enjoyable and all very good for the theater.

But regardless of the formative experimentation, the volume of the music and the diversity of the cast, "Passing Strange" really is just as traditionally sentimental a show as something by Jerry Herman.
anthemic songs and a script full of zingers
It rattles your bones and seizes your soul in ways that no recent Broadway rock musical, including last season's Spring Awakening, could even conceive.
Passing Strange is a soul-stirring musical memoir about a young black artist's journey of self-discovery that pulses with the authentic voice of someone who has lived to tell his tale.
It’s an enjoyable show but a frustrating one, never quite fulfilling its promise.
This universal theme is explored in numerous ways during the evening culminating with a resounding wisdom that is effectively original, but more often simply mesmerizing.
